Abstract. Sepsis is a life-threatening condition, caused by the body’s extreme response to
an infection. In the United States, 1.7 million cases of sepsis occur annually, resulting in
265,000 deaths. Delayed diagnosis and treatment are associated with higher mortality rates.
An exponential rise in the availability of medical data has allowed for the development of
sophisticated machine learning algorithms to predict sepsis earlier than the onset. How-
ever, these models often underperform, as the training data are retrospective and do not
fully capture the uncertain future. In this study, we develop a novel framework, which we
refer to as MLePOMDP, to leverage and combine the underlying, high-level knowledge
about sepsis progression and machine learning (ML) for classification. Specifically, we use
a hidden Markov model to describe sepsis development at a high level, where the ML
model makes the higher-order “observations” from temporal data. Consequently, a par-
tially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) model is developed to make classifi-
cation decisions. We analytically establish that the optimal policy is of threshold-type,
which we exploit to efficiently optimize MLePOMDP. MLePOMDP is calibrated and tested
using high-frequency physiological data collected from bedside monitors. Different from
past POMDP-based frameworks, MLePOMDP is developed for a prediction task using a
very small state definition, produces highly interpretable results, and accounts for a novel
and clinically meaningful action space. Our results show that MLePOMDP outperforms

the generalizability of MLePOMDP to different patient cohorts.
Summary of Contribution: This study develops a novel real-time decision support frame-
work for early sepsis prediction by integrating well-known machine learning models (ran-
dom forest and neural networks) with a well-established sequential decision-making
model, namely, a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). The structural
properties of the optimal policy are further explored and a threshold-type structure is
established, which is then leveraged to develop a customized algorithm to solve the prob-
lem more efficiently. The resulting framework demonstrates the benefit of applying
POMDPs to augment machine learning outputs. Specifically, the framework results in the
reduction of false alarms in sepsis predictions where decisions are made in real time, hence
improving the overall prediction precision.

A majority of the existing work involves developing
machine learning (ML) algorithms to predict whether
a patient would develop sepsis (Islam et al. 2019, Fleu-
ren et al. 2020, Moor et al. 2021). Among the algo-
rithms, many have used proof-of-concept methods
where sepsis prediction has occurred as a one-time
decision (e.g., Desautels et al. 2016, Taylor et al. 2016,
McCoy and Das 2017, Shashikumar et al. 2017, van
Wyk et al. 2017, Khojandi et al. 2018b, Wang et al.
2018, Barton et al. 2019, Chiew et al. 2019), whereas
others have taken a step further to develop ML-based
algorithms for potential real-time implementation
(e.g., Gultepe et al. 2014; Henry et al. 2015; Calvert
et al. 2016; Futoma et al. 2017; Khoshnevisan et al.
2018; Lin et al. 2018; Nemati et al. 2018; Fagerstro¨m
et al. 2019; Moor et al. 2019; van Wyk et al. 2019a,b;
Kok et al. 2020; Liu et al. 2021; Rafiei et al. 2021; Sha-
shikumar et al. 2021). New advances regarding the lat-
ter have been partly fueled by the 2019 PhysioNet
Computing in Cardiology Challenge (e.g., Abromavi-
cius et al. 2020, He et al. 2020, Nesaragi and Patidar
2020, Reyna et al. 2020).
Although significant advancements were made in
early sepsis prediction by adopting ML techniques, it
is important to acknowledge the inherent shortcom-
ings of ML algorithms. Data used to train ML models
for prediction are by necessity reliant on retrospective
data. Because these models learn from historical data,
they often fail to generalize well to new unseen data,
especially when the environments in which the mod-
els are deployed change dynamically (Haas et al.
2011). Another major pitfall of ML-based predictions
is that no matter how complex the predictive model,
prescriptive decisions are still made using threshold-
based methods. For instance, in a classification prob-
lem using ML methods, such as random forest (RF) or
neural network (NN), it is common to classify an
input to the class with the maximal confidence (Hastie
et al. 2017). Particularly, in sepsis prediction problems,
an ML model predicts a “probability” that a patient
has sepsis. Then, the probability is compared with an
a priori threshold (typically 0.5) to classify the subject
as a sepsis/nonsepsis patient.
As a result, current sepsis prediction methods often
suffer from low specificity (true negative rate), espe-
cially when implemented in real time (Giuliano 2007,
Gultepe et al. 2014, Henry et al. 2015, Shashikumar
et al. 2017, Chiew et al. 2019, Islam et al. 2019). This is
mainly because the imposed threshold is not flexible
enough to filter out false positives, resulting in a rela-
tively high false alarm rate. Excessive false alarms
could cause alarm fatigue, which contributed to 566
deaths in the United States from 2005 to 2008 (Cvach
2012). Alarm fatigue is especially harmful in a cohort
with unbalanced classes. The prevalence of sepsis in

(Rhee et al. 2017,
Sakr et al. 2018). As such, given the unbalanced ratio
of sepsis to nonsepsis patients, even a moderate false
positive rate can cause a significant number of false
alarms (Saito and Rehmsmeier 2015). Hence, before
the adoption of sepsis detection algorithms as part of
early warning systems in hospitals, it is important to
develop real-time algorithms that are not only highly
sensitive but also particularly specific and precise (i.e.,
present a low false alarm rate).

prediction framework that addresses two shortcom-

dynamically changing circumstances and their reli-
ance on an a priori threshold. This novel framework
embeds an ML-based predictive model into a pre-
scriptive model to make classification decisions. Spe-
cifically, we develop an ML-based predictive model
and integrate it into a partially observable Markov
decision process (POMDP) model.
We refer to this ML-enabled POMDP framework as
MLePOMDP. In MLePOMDP, the ML model “peeks”
into the hidden state of the patient in real time through
ML-based “observations,” while simultaneously ac-
counting for the patient’s underlying disease pro-
gression at a high level to construct an accurate
understanding of his or her health state to enable im-
proved decision making. The “decisions” are “pre-
dictions” of the future state of the patient, made based
on the temporal changes in high-frequency bedside
monitor data. These decisions would draw the atten-
tion of the ICU bedside staff to at-risk patients as early
as possible, while ensuring enough confidence in them
to avoid false alarms.
Our proposed MLePOMDP models sepsis progres-
sion at a high level using binary states and embeds
ML into Markov models to address sepsis prediction.

perhaps the most closely related works to ours are
those that jointly use ML and Markov models to pre-

network (RNN), resulting in hundreds of states. This
results in a lack of interpretability in the model out-
put. In contrast, in this study, we create a novel way
of integrating ML and Markov models for sepsis pre-
diction that keeps the state definition very small. This
makes the model amenable to structural analysis and
provides interpretability and explainability, which are
extremely important for early warning systems.

2. Model Formulation
We consider the development of sepsis in the human
body as a stochastically evolving system, where the
ground truth of sepsis is unknown to an outside
observer. A traditional ML model, which only relies
on historical data to predict the future, lacks a com-
prehensive understanding of the system dynamics
and its future evolution. To improve model perform-
ance, we provide the model with knowledge of the
future by assuming that the underlying state of the
system evolves according to a Markov chain (Karlin
and Taylor 1975). As such, we can capture the com-
plex dynamics of the system using a higher-order hid-
den Markov model (HOHMM) (Hadar and Messer
2009). However, it is generally difficult to estimate the
parameters of these models. Therefore, we instead
exploit ML to capture the complex interactions of fea-
tures from high-dimensional data sets and use ML
predictions to construct a first-order hidden Markov
model (HMM) (Krishnamurthy 2016).
In a first-order HMM, the future evolution of the
system depends on the past only through the current
state, and the underlying health state of the patient
(sepsis or nonsepsis) can only be inferred through
observations. To make observations, we use an ML
model on the raw multichannel physiological data
streams to obtain “aggregated predictions” about the
underlying state of the system. Note that, as in most
ML models, these predictions (now observations for
HMM) are not necessarily accurate. Therefore, we use
these observations in the HMM to update belief states
over time and develop a POMDP model to determine
the optimal predictions for the system, overall enhanc-
ing the predictive power of the embedded ML model.

2. Model Formulation
We consider the development of sepsis in the human
body as a stochastically evolving system, where the
ground truth of sepsis is unknown to an outside
observer. A traditional ML model, which only relies
on historical data to predict the future, lacks a com-
prehensive understanding of the system dynamics
and its future evolution. To improve model perform-
ance, we provide the model with knowledge of the
future by assuming that the underlying state of the
system evolves according to a Markov chain (Karlin
and Taylor 1975). As such, we can capture the com-
plex dynamics of the system using a higher-order hid-
den Markov model (HOHMM) (Hadar and Messer
2009). However, it is generally difficult to estimate the
parameters of these models. Therefore, we instead
exploit ML to capture the complex interactions of fea-
tures from high-dimensional data sets and use ML
predictions to construct a first-order hidden Markov
model (HMM) (Krishnamurthy 2016).
In a first-order HMM, the future evolution of the
system depends on the past only through the current
state, and the underlying health state of the patient
(sepsis or nonsepsis) can only be inferred through
observations. To make observations, we use an ML
model on the raw multichannel physiological data
streams to obtain “aggregated predictions” about the
underlying state of the system. Note that, as in most
ML models, these predictions (now observations for
HMM) are not necessarily accurate. Therefore, we use
these observations in the HMM to update belief states
over time and develop a POMDP model to determine
the optimal predictions for the system, overall enhanc-
ing the predictive power of the embedded ML model.
Figure 1 demonstrates an overview of MLePOMDP.
For the sake of simplicity, we present MLePOMDP in
two stages. In the first stage, temporal data from the
system are used by a trained ML model to make a pre-
diction about the current system state. These pre-
dictions are fed to a second-stage POMDP model as
partial observations. The observations are used to
update the belief about the state of the system. Actions
are taken based on the belief and generate immediate
rewards/costs. The system then continues to evolve,
and the process continues. The goal is to identify the
optimal policy that maximizes the total expected
reward generated by the system.

In general, MLePOMDP is very flexible. It allows
for a large class of ML models to be integrated into
POMDPs, as long as the outputs of the ML models are
treated as observations of hidden systems. In addi-
tion, MLePOMDP expands the capability of Markov
models. Traditionally, Markov models are widely
used to solve problems with limited system states or
observations in each state, mainly to reduce the com-
putational burden (Langville and Stewart 2004, Lin
et al. 2004, Sleptchenko and Johnson 2015, Khojandi
et al. 2018a). However, with the help of ML models,
MLePOMDP is able to take high-dimensional data as
input, where the number of features considered
imposes no computational burden on the Markov
models themselves. This is because, in MLePOMDP,
ML models first extract vital information from high-
dimensional data, which POMDPs use to make
“informed” decisions while accounting for the knowl-
edge of system dynamics.
2.1. First-Stage Model
To develop ML models for real-time detection of sep-
sis in multichannel high-frequency data streams, we
use overlapping sliding time windows introduced in
previous studies (van Wyk et al. 2019a, b; Liu et al.
2021). Specifically, we extract features using three
time windows of length 0.25 hour, 0.5 hour, and 1
hour, applied to the physiological data and moving
forward every minute, until one hour before sepsis
onset. For each of the time windows, mean, minimum,
maximum, standard deviation, variance, skewness,
kurtosis, and slope (per best-fitting line using linear
regression) are extracted from four vital signs: heart
rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), blood pressure (BP),
and oxygen saturation
({\mathrm{SpO}}_{2})
. Additionally, for HR,
RR, and BP, entropy is calculated with the one-hour
time window. After preprocessing, a total of 144 fea-
tures are extracted from patients’ physiological data at
each time epoch.
In this study, we use random forest (RF) and neural
network (NN) as our ML-based prediction models.
Note that we also consider RNNs as an alternative;
however, because the results are ultimately unfavora-
ble, we only include the details about these models in
Online Appendix A.
RF is a supervised ML model that ensembles multi-
ple decision trees. The probability of sepsis is calcu-
lated as the mean predicted sepsis probabilities of the
trees in the forest. RF is generally robust against over-
fitting and requires little hyperparameter tuning. One
of the most important parameters to tune in RF is the
number of trees in the forest, which is optimized
according to the out-of-bag (OOB) error (Breiman
2001). Additionally, we train a fully connected NN as
an alternative first-stage model. Specifically, we con-
struct the NN as a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with
one neuron in the output layer so that the output rep-
resents the probability of sepsis. NN can model highly
nonlinear relationships between variables; however, it
generally requires extensive efforts in hyperparameter
tuning to achieve good performance while remaining
generalizable. As such, the NN structure is selected
using a 10-fold cross-validation based on the cross-
entropy loss.
For both the RF and the NN models, predictions are
made every minute, starting from hour 1, through the
end of the horizon. Note that, because a window-
based approach to extract features is used, the first
prediction is made one hour (equal to the length of
the largest window) after the beginning of the
observation horizon. The stream of predicted proba-
bilities of sepsis is used as observations in the sec-
ond stage.

4. Solution Approach
In this section, we discuss the solution approach in
both the first and second stages. Specifically, we
describe an existing solution approach for the second-
stage POMDP model and then outline how we incor-
porate the structural properties established in Section
3 into the solution algorithm to improve its efficiency.
Note that MLePOMDP is extremely flexible, allow-
ing for any predictive model (first stage) to be paired
and integrated with the decision-making process (sec-
ond stage) to solve real-time classification tasks that
involve stochastically evolving systems. However,
this flexibility does not complicate the solution
approach, as the two stages can be modeled and opti-
mized individually. Specifically, the first-stage ML
model can be developed and optimized using an
array of existing machine learning libraries. In our
case study, ML models are implemented and opti-
mized using the Python scikit-learn library (Oliphant
2007, Pedregosa et al. 2011). The NN model is trained
with the Adam algorithm (Kingma and Ba 2014).
Solving a POMDP model is challenging. Various
classes of exact and approximate solution methods exist
for POMDPs. Exact solution algorithms can solve small
instances of POMDP models to optimality, for example,
Monahan’s algorithm, Sondik’s algorithm, and the wit-
ness algorithm (Krishnamurthy 2016). However, solv-
ing models with extremely large policy spaces using
exact approaches is often intractable due to the curse of
dimensionality (Roy et al. 2005). Approximate methods
can mitigate this problem. These methods include the
MDP-based approximations such as point-based value
iteration (PBVI) (Pineau et al. 2003, Spaan and Vlassis
2005), grid-based approximations (Zhou and Hansen
2001, Bonet 2002) and other hybrid heuristic methods
(Lin et al. 2004). In addition, cutting-edge artificial intel-
ligence (AI) techniques, such as reinforcement learning
(RL) (Kunnumkal and Topaloglu 2008, Wang et al.
2019), can also be used to solve large-scale POMDP
problems. There are also specialized algorithms that
solve optimal stopping POMDPs, such as a linear
approximation algorithm that estimates the stopping
threshold (Krishnamurthy 2011). However, due to siz-
able differences in model formulations, especially in
the reward structure and special properties required in
the observation probability matrix, assumptions made
in the established algorithms are not fully satisfied in
our second-stage POMDP. Thus, it is difficult to
directly apply the algorithms in the literature to this
study.
Per our preliminary experiments, using exact algo-
rithms to solve the second-stage POMDP model is too
time-consuming. Thus, we propose a modified PBVI
algorithm to solve this POMDP model. The PBVI algo-

backup and belief point set expansion. As such,
instead of evaluating all the beliefs in the belief space,
the algorithm only focuses on the belief points that are
important to the solution structure. The PBVI algo-
rithm produces “good enough” solutions with less
computational time.

5.1. Data
We use two separate data sources in this study. We
refer to these data sets as “ICU data” and “eICU data.”
In the following, we describe these data sets in detail.
We collect physiological data in six distinct ICU facili-
ties from a large hospital system in the southeastern
region of the United States, using the proprietary
Cerner CareAware iBus platform (Cerner Corporation
2018). In the following, we use “ICU data” to refer to
this data set. Only basic vital signs are included in this
study: HR, RR, (mean, systolic, and diastolic) noninva-
sive BP, and
{\mathrm{SpO}}_{2}
. A majority of the vital signs are
captured on a minute-by-minute basis. In rare cases,
when blood pressure values are collected with lower
frequencies, the data are imputed with the last obser-
vation carried forward (LOCF). Through the study,
we follow the ethical principles from the Declaration
of Helsinki for medical research involving human sub-
jects. This study was reviewed properly by the Institu-
tional Review Board at the University of Tennessee
Health Science Center (21-08088-XP). Sepsis is defined
using the Sepsis-3 criteria (Singer et al. 2016). Patient
characteristics of the ICU data are summarized in
Online Appendix D (available online).
From the ICU data, two data sets were created with
different lengths of the observation horizon. The first
data set contains data starting from seven hours before
sepsis onset until one hour before sepsis onset, with a
horizon of six hours. The second data set contains
data from 11 hours before sepsis onset until one hour
before onset, with a horizon of 10 hours. The former
data set has 441 sepsis and 441 nonsepsis patients, and
the latter has 317 sepsis and 317 nonsepsis patients.
In order to externally validate MLePOMDP per-
formance, we employ the eICU Collaborative Research
Database (Pollard et al. 2018), a database containing
patient cohorts from various hospitals that are admit-
ted to the ICU during 2014–2015. To ensure feasibility
as well as generalizability, we bootstrap 10 smaller
data sets from the entire eICU database, each contain-
ing 500 sepsis and 500 nonsepsis patients, with six-
hour observation horizons. Patient data are collected
until one hour before sepsis onset. We use the term
“eICU data” to refer to this data set. Different from the
ICU data, which are generally collected on a minute-by-
minute basis, HR and RR in the eICU data are
collected every five minutes and noninvasive BPs are
collected aperiodically. The data collected with fre-
quencies lower than five minutes are imputed with
LOCF. Diagnosis of sepsis and its time of onset are
identified in a similar manner as in the ICU data.
Source codes for the eICU experiment can be found
online (https://github.com/ILABUTK/MLePOMDP_
Early_Sepsis_Detection).

5.3. Benchmark
We compare the performance of MLePOMDP with
models developed using standard ML. In this study,
we use RF and NN as the first-stage model. As dis-
cussed in Section 2.1, we also conduct experiments
where we consider RNNs, especially long short-term
memory (LSTM) networks. The results are overall
unfavorable for our cohort, compared with RF and
NN results, and, hence, we only include these results
in Online Appendix A.
In this study, experiments are conducted in a real-
time fashion, where actions are taken in every decision
epoch throughout the observation horizon (for com-
pleteness, the “snapshot” first-stage ML model per-
formances measured at static timestamps are shown in
Online Appendix E). The benchmark method repre-
sents decision making in a traditional ML classification
model (e.g., based on RF or NN), where decisions are
made by applying a 0.5 threshold to the predicted
probability. To implement the ML models, we apply a
0.5 threshold to the first-stage output. If/when the
probability is larger than 0.5, we classify the patient as
septic and the process terminates. Six metrics are con-
sidered to evaluate performance: Sensitivity, specificity,
precision, F1 score, area under the curve (AUC), and
“lead time to sepsis.” Note that the AUC is only calcu-
lated to evaluate the performance of the first-stage ML
models, since the second-stage POMDP makes sepsis/
nonsepsis decisions directly and does not have an
adjustable threshold to produce AUC. Also, note that
we define “lead time to sepsis” as the length of time
between when a model makes a sepsis diagnosis for a
patient and the time of sepsis as marked by Sepsis-3
definition. In Online Appendix F, we present the results
of the changes in this lead time as a function of the clas-
sification threshold used in the ML models.
We design experiments to compare the perform-
ance of MLePOMDP with that of the benchmark. Spe-
cifically, we investigate the impact of the choice of ML
model (RF vs. NN), the ratio of sepsis to nonsepsis
patients (1:1 vs. 1:3), and the decision-making interval
for the POMDP model as part of the two-stage frame-
work (one minute vs. five minutes). In the following
sections, we only show the results from data sets with
six-hour observation horizons. The performance met-
rics for the 10-hour observation horizon data sets are
summarized in Online Appendix G. In addition, we
present results of a sensitivity analysis on the second-
stage policy in Online Appendix H, using various
reward structures.

We compare the performance of MLePOMDP with
models developed using standard ML. In this study,
we use RF and NN as the first-stage model. As dis-

where we consider RNNs, especially long short-term

unfavorable for our cohort, compared with RF and

in Online Appendix A.
In this study, experiments are conducted in a real-
time fashion, where actions are taken in every decision
epoch throughout the observation horizon (for com-
pleteness, the “snapshot” first-stage ML model per-
formances measured at static timestamps are shown in
Online Appendix E). The benchmark method repre-
sents decision making in a traditional ML classification
model (e.g., based on RF or NN), where decisions are
made by applying a 0.5 threshold to the predicted
probability. To implement the ML models, we apply a
0.5 threshold to the first-stage output. If/when the
probability is larger than 0.5, we classify the patient as
septic and the process terminates. Six metrics are con-
sidered to evaluate performance: Sensitivity, specificity,
precision, F1 score, area under the curve (AUC), and
“lead time to sepsis.” Note that the AUC is only calcu-
lated to evaluate the performance of the first-stage ML
models, since the second-stage POMDP makes sepsis/
nonsepsis decisions directly and does not have an
adjustable threshold to produce AUC. Also, note that
we define “lead time to sepsis” as the length of time
between when a model makes a sepsis diagnosis for a
patient and the time of sepsis as marked by Sepsis-3
definition. In Online Appendix F, we present the results
of the changes in this lead time as a function of the clas-
sification threshold used in the ML models.

improve patient (and alarm) management.

developed to make such predictions from real-time data.

integrate these ML-estimated probabilities within a
probabilistic model to improve the overall performance.
Similarly, MLePODMP can be applied in other applica-

and used to make predictions about the state of a sys-
tem, such as anomaly detection (Watts 2021) and
machine maintenance (Susto et al. 2015). Further, it is
also possible to extend MLePOMDP to multiclass classi-

can be viewed as classification with increased class gran-
ularity. In this case, the ML models predict probabil-

decisions about the correct classes according to the ML
outputs. As such, potential applications include, but are
not limited to, weather forecasting (Hewage et al. 2020),
financial management (Lopez de Prado 2018), and energy
systems (Heidari and Khovalyg 2020).
